rq: Is air connectivity clean connectivity? Trade and openness have ambiguous effects on the environment because scale, composition and technique effects pull in different directions (Grossman and Krueger 1993; Antweiler, Copeland and Taylor 2001; Managi, Hibiki and Tsurumi 2009). This paper asks a narrower question: when a country becomes more central in the global air network, does the pollution and carbon intensity of its economy fall, and if so through which of the three channels?

Air connectivity is measured with the Global Air Connectivity Index (GACI), a within-year standardised composite of degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector and regional-importance centrality of each airport, aggregated to the country by seat-weighted mean. Because aviation itself emits under 3% of national CO2 and a negligible share of SO2, any effect on national intensities must run through the economy, not through aircraft.

Hypotheses. H1 (clean connectivity): higher air connectivity lowers SO2, NOx and CO2 per unit of GDP and raises the renewable share. H2 (technique, not composition): the reduction occurs within fuels, as lower emissions per unit of fuel burned, and is not explained by shifts in industrial structure. H3 (where): the effect is concentrated in goods-producing economies that have plants and power stations to retrofit, not in service economies.

Design. Country-year panel, 149 countries, 1996–2019 (unified sample). ln y = b ln GACI + ln pop + ln GDP pc + (ln GDP pc)^2 + country FE + year FE, standard errors clustered by country. Tables 1–4 and the Appendix are fixed-effects OLS. Table 5 is instrumental variables: GACI is instrumented by Feyrer-type air market access, which interacts a country's fixed geography (its great-circle distances to all other markets relative to sea distances) with the world-wide growth of air traffic, so that it moves only with global technology and not with the country's own policies or outcomes; the second instrument, UNESCO natural and mixed heritage sites times world tourist arrivals, is weak in this sample and enters only the over-identified model. The GACI coefficient is an elasticity; one within-country standard deviation of ln GACI is 0.07, so a one-SD move changes an outcome by about 7% of the coefficient.
T1: Air connectivity is associated with cleaner production per unit of GDP: a 1% higher GACI lowers SO2 intensity by about 0.9% and NOx intensity by 0.3%, raises the renewable share by 8 points per log unit, and lowers CO2 and energy intensity by about 0.3%. The fuel mix (CO2 per unit of energy) does not move. One within-country SD of connectivity translates into 7% lower SO2 intensity and 2 to 3% lower carbon and energy intensity. The income terms trace the usual inverted-U Kuznets curve. Panel B instruments ln GACI with Feyrer-type air market access (first-stage F 12.5): every sign is confirmed and the SO2, NOx, renewable and CO2-intensity effects remain significant. The IV coefficients are about six times the OLS ones, which is expected when the regressor is a noisy within-year relative index (attenuation in OLS) but also means the IV magnitudes should not be read literally; one within-SD would imply a 40% fall in SO2 intensity.
T2: The SO2 reduction is a technique effect in the Antweiler–Copeland–Taylor sense: coal combustion does not fall (if anything it rises), yet SO2 emitted per unit of coal and oil burned falls by roughly 1% per 1% of GACI. Because a fuel's emission factor depends only on its sulphur content and on end-of-pipe desulphurisation, this isolates abatement technology and fuel standards. Process SO2 from smelters and refineries, whose location is fixed by geology, does not respond, which serves as a placebo. Panel B: the IV confirms the technique pattern where the instrument has power. SO2 per unit of oil falls (−7.5, F 12.6) and process SO2 and the coal share do not move; in the coal-using subsamples the instrument is weak (F 3–5) and the coal-emission-factor IV estimate is imprecise.
T3: Adding industrial composition (manufacturing, services, agriculture shares), openness (trade, FDI) and urbanisation barely moves the GACI coefficient: in the OLS panel all observable channels together account for under 10% of it, and composition alone for 2–9%. Panel B repeats the decomposition for the 2SLS coefficient, with the mediator auxiliary regressions also estimated by 2SLS so that the identity holds exactly. The conclusion is the same: composition explains at most 10% (and has the wrong sign for SO2), and the full IV coefficient is in fact larger in magnitude than the base one, because connectivity raises trade and FDI, which are associated with higher SO2 and NOx intensity, so openness masks part of the clean effect rather than explaining it. The composition channel emphasised in the pollution-haven literature is not what drives the result; combined with Table 2 this leaves technique as the operative channel.
T4: The clean-connectivity effect lives in goods-producing economies: in countries with above-median merchandise trade in 1996 the GACI coefficients on NOx, renewables and CO2 intensity are large and significant, while in service economies they are zero or positive. By income, the SO2 effect is concentrated in the low-income tercile. Both patterns fit a story of technology and standards reaching industrial economies that still have abatement to install, and do not fit a tourism-pressure story. Panel B splits the IV by economy type: in goods economies the IV point estimates are large and negative for SO2 and NOx and positive for renewables, with the same ordering as OLS, but the subsample first stages are weak (F 5.1 goods, 2.8 services) so the split-sample IV is suggestive only. Tercile-level IV is not reported: within the low- and mid-income terciles the instrument has no first-stage power.
T5: This table collects the IV diagnostics behind the Panel B estimates. With air market access alone (F 12.5) the estimates are those reported in the Panel B rows. Adding the heritage-times-tourism instrument, which has no first-stage power in this sample, changes little; the Sargan test does not reject for SO2, renewables and CO2 intensity but rejects for NOx. We treat the IV as evidence on direction, not as the preferred magnitude.
A1a: The SO2 result survives adding capital-labour ratio and trade openness (Managi et al. controls) and a geographic sea-connectivity control, and is strongest in 1996–2009. It weakens and loses significance when the comparison is restricted within region-years or within income-group-years, when liner shipping connectivity (2006–) is added, and in 2010–2019. GACI is a relative, within-year index, so these stricter designs remove much of its variation; we report them as the boundary of what the country panel can identify.
A1b: The CO2-intensity result is weaker and less stable than the SO2 result: it is robust to Managi-style controls and to the sea-connectivity control, becomes stronger with LSCI in the 2006+ window and in 2010–2019, but is zero under region-by-year or income-group-by-year effects. CO2 is the expected weak outcome of the mechanism: desulphurisation does not reduce CO2, and the only CO2 channel we find is energy efficiency (Table 1).
A2: Results are not an artefact of the aggregation rule. The seat-weighted mean of airport GACI (used throughout) and its level give the same picture; the unweighted mean across all airports is smaller and insignificant, because it dilutes hub airports with many small ones. Connectivity of the airports that carry traffic is what matters.
why: Openness reaches a country through two physical networks that carry different things. Ships move goods: over 80% of world trade by volume travels by sea, and the goods that travel by sea are the heavy, energy- and pollution-intensive ones (ores, fuels, steel, chemicals, cement). Aircraft move people and ideas: almost all intercontinental passenger travel is by air, and air cargo is about a third of world trade by value but under one percent by weight (IATA), concentrated in electronics, pharmaceuticals and precision machinery. The trade-and-environment literature measures openness with trade volumes, which bundle these two networks together and therefore cannot tell whether the environmental effect of openness comes from the goods that arrive by ship or from the people and knowledge that arrive by plane.

Air connectivity isolates the people-and-knowledge channel. Business travel is a documented engine of technology diffusion (Hovhannisyan and Keller 2015), new direct air links raise firm-to-firm connections and local growth (Campante and Yanagizawa-Drott 2018), face-to-face contact is necessary for trading complex goods and services (Cristea 2011), and the opening of airspace increased trade in exactly the goods that need in-person coordination (Söderlund 2023). Abatement technology is this kind of knowledge: flue-gas desulphurisation, low-sulphur refining, combined-cycle plants and wind and solar projects are installed by vendors, engineers, consultants and financiers who travel, and the standards that mandate them are copied by regulators who meet. If air connectivity transmits anything to the environment, the technique effect is where it should appear.

The question matters for policy because aviation is regulated for its own emissions. Ticket taxes, ETS coverage and route restrictions are justified by aircraft CO2, which is about 2.5% of the global total. Our companion paper on European aviation taxes finds that these taxes reduce seats and connectivity at small airports. Whether that is a net environmental gain depends on whether connectivity has an economy-wide clean effect that the aircraft-only accounting omits. For developing countries the same question arises in reverse: open-skies agreements and airport investment are evaluated on tourism and trade, and an environmental co-benefit through faster adoption of clean technology would change that evaluation.

GACI is the right measure for this question because it captures a country's position in the network, not the volume of its traffic. It is a within-year standardised composite of degree, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector and regional-importance centrality of each airport, so a country's value rises when its airports become better connected to the rest of the network relative to other countries' airports. That is the relevant object for knowledge flows: what matters is who a country's firms, engineers and officials can reach in a day, not how many seats depart. Seat volume (Appendix Table 2) and the geographic sea-connectivity controls (Appendix Table 1) are reported to show that the results come from network position rather than from traffic or from maritime access.
gaci_title: What GACI is and how to read it

gaci.text: GACI (Global Air Connectivity Index) is an airport-level index of position in the world air network, built from OAG scheduled-service data for about 3,500 airports a year, 1996–2024. For each year the scheduled network is a weighted graph: nodes are airports, edges are routes, edge weights are seat capacity. Five centrality measures are computed for every airport: degree (number of destinations), flow betweenness (how much indirect traffic routes through the airport, the hub measure), closeness (how few connections are needed to reach the rest of the network), eigenvector centrality (connection to other well-connected airports) and regional importance (the airport's share of its region's capacity). Figure 1(a) illustrates the objects on a toy network; a hub such as HKG scores high on betweenness because flows between Europe and Australasia pass through it.

The five measures are combined by principal components within each year. Figure 1(b) shows that the first component carries 73–77% of the variance and loads almost equally on the five measures (weights 0.38–0.49) in every year, so GACI is in effect an equally weighted standardised average of the five centralities. Because the PCA is run year by year on standardised inputs, GACI is a relative measure: it tells us where an airport stands in that year's network, not how many flights it has. An airport whose traffic grows at the world average rate keeps a constant GACI; GACI rises only when the airport becomes more central relative to others.
gaci.cap: Figure 1. Construction of GACI. (a) Network objects on a toy graph. (b) Year-by-year first-principal-component loadings and variance share, 1996–2023.

gaci.text: For the country-level analysis we take the seat-weighted mean of GACI across a country's airports (cwm) and use its log. Weighting by seats means the index describes the airports that actually carry the country's traffic; Appendix Table 2 shows that the unweighted mean, which gives a small regional field the same weight as the main hub, is a weaker regressor. Figure 2 shows the country series for six economies. Germany and the United States are flat, because their position was already central and grew with the world. The UAE, Türkiye, China and Ethiopia rise steeply as Dubai, Istanbul, the Chinese secondary cities and Addis Ababa became hubs. This is the within-country variation the fixed-effects regressions use: a country's GACI changes when its network position changes relative to the rest of the world.
gaci.cap: Figure 2. ln GACI (seat-weighted country mean) for six countries, 1996–2019.

gaci.text: Two consequences for reading the tables. First, the within-country standard deviation of ln GACI is small, 0.07, because most countries' relative position moves slowly; coefficients therefore look large per log unit and should be read as effects of a 7% change in connectivity, which is roughly what Türkiye or China achieved in a typical five-year window. Second, because GACI is relative and within-year standardised, designs that compare countries only within their own region-year or income-group-year remove much of its variation (Appendix Table 1); we report them as the boundary of the country panel.

Figure 3 shows the main result as a binned scatter. Both axes are residuals after country and year fixed effects and the income and population controls (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell), so each point is the mean of about 140 country-years with similar connectivity residuals. The downward slope in panel (a) is the Table 1 coefficient on SO2 intensity; panel (b) shows the same relation for SO2 per unit of oil burned, the emission-factor outcome of Table 2 that isolates the technique effect. The relation is approximately linear and is not driven by a few extreme bins.
gaci.cap: Figure 3. Binned scatter of the within-country relation between ln GACI and (a) ln SO2/GDP, (b) ln SO2 per unit of oil CO2. Unified sample, 25 bins; line is the regression slope.

gaci.text: Figure 4 maps the tables onto the scale–composition–technique decomposition that organises the paper. Scale and composition are tested and rejected in Tables 2 and 3; technique is where the effect appears. Table 4 says where (goods-producing economies), Table 5 confirms the direction with an instrument.
gaci.cap: Figure 4. Which table tests which channel.

agg_title: Global aggregate: what the elasticity implies

agg.text: Figure 5 puts the two sides of the result on a map. Panel (a) is the change in ln GACI between the first and last year a country appears in the unified sample (1996 to 2019 for most). Connectivity gains were largest in the Gulf, Türkiye, China, Korea and Eastern Europe, and were negative in parts of Latin America, the Sahel and conflict countries (Syria, Yemen, Venezuela). Panel (b) is the observed change in ln SO2/GDP over the same window. The two maps are mirror images in East Asia, the Gulf and Europe, where connectivity rose and SO2 intensity collapsed; they also agree in the countries where connectivity fell and SO2 intensity did not improve.
agg.cap: Figure 5. (a) Change in ln GACI and (b) observed change in ln SO2/GDP, first to last sample year. Grey: outside the unified sample.

agg.text: A back-of-the-envelope aggregate follows from the Table 1 elasticity. Holding each country's connectivity at its initial level and applying the point estimate of −0.94 to its observed change in ln GACI, SO2 emissions in the final year would have been about 19 Mt higher than observed, which is 28% of final-year SO2 in the sample and roughly half of the 37 Mt decline recorded between 1996 and 2019. The 95% band is wide, from 3 Mt (9% of the decline) to 41 Mt, because the elasticity is estimated with a standard error of 0.38. By region the implied reduction in SO2 intensity is 18–19% in Asia and Europe, 15% in the Middle East, 6–8% in Africa and Latin America; in tonnes it is dominated by China (7.2 Mt), India, Russia, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.

This exercise is an accounting illustration, not a causal decomposition of the global SO2 decline: it extrapolates a within-country elasticity linearly to changes two to three times the within-country standard deviation, and it attributes to connectivity whatever the fixed-effects regression attributes to it. Its purpose is to show that the coefficient is economically meaningful at the scale of the actual network changes of the period, not that air connectivity explains half of global desulphurisation.
